whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Sharing and Visibility Architect exam for?

personas.label: Security-Focused Admins
personas.description: You already set up profiles, roles and sharing rules, and you want to learn how to design a sharing model for a large org from the start.

personas.label: Platform Architects
personas.description: Sharing and Visibility Architect is one of the four exams you need for Application Architect, so it sits on most architect paths.

personas.label: Compliance Specialists
personas.description: You need to prove who can see which records, and explain why, to auditors or security teams.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Sharing and Visibility Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It is harder than it looks. Most questions describe a user who can or can't see a record, and you have to work out which layer is causing it: org-wide defaults, the role hierarchy, sharing rules, teams, or something in code.
bullets: 67% to pass, which is about 41 correct answers. Many questions have two answers that look right and differ by one sharing setting.
External users trip people up. Experience Cloud sharing sets, external org-wide defaults and guest user rules come up often.
Performance is tested too. Know what makes sharing recalculation slow, such as data skew and very deep role hierarchies.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: You will do best if you have designed a sharing model for a real org, not just added a sharing rule here and there. Before you book, aim for 75% or more on practice tests and be able to explain, step by step, why a user can see a record.

examFormat.heading: Sharing and Visibility Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Almost every question is a short scenario. A typical one says a group of users needs to see some records but not others, then asks for the simplest setup that does it without opening up too much access.
bestWayToPass: Start from the most locked-down setting: Set org-wide defaults to the most private level anyone needs, then open access up with roles and rules. The exam favours this approach.
Separate object, field and record access: Profiles and permission sets control objects and fields. Sharing controls which records. Many wrong answers mix these up.
Study external sharing on its own: Partner and customer users follow different rules from internal users. Learn sharing sets, share groups and external defaults.
Know when code is needed: Apex managed sharing is the answer only when declarative sharing can't express the rule.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you design who can see and edit which data in Salesforce. You choose org-wide defaults, roles, sharing rules and permission sets, and you plan for external users and large data volumes.

keyConcepts.h2: Sharing and Visibility Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: OWD and the Security Baseline
blocks.body: Org-wide defaults (OWD) set the starting level of record access for each object: Private, Public Read Only or Public Read/Write. Everything else can only add access on top of OWD, never take it away. So the rule is simple: set OWD to the most restricted level any user needs, then open access up for the people who need more. For child objects in a master-detail relationship, the setting is Controlled by Parent. Internal and external users can have different defaults, and the external default can't be more open than the internal one.

blocks.heading: Record Sharing: Role Hierarchy, Rules, and Manual Sharing
blocks.body: The **role hierarchy** lets managers see the records their team owns. You can turn this off for custom objects with Grant Access Using Hierarchies. **Owner-based sharing rules** share records owned by one group with another group. **Criteria-based sharing rules** share records based on a field value, such as Region equals EMEA. **Account, Opportunity and Case teams** give access to named people on a single record. **Manual sharing** lets a record owner share one record with someone, but it is removed if the owner changes. **Apex managed sharing** covers the rules none of these can handle, and it survives an owner change.

blocks.heading: External User Sharing: Communities and Partner Portals
blocks.body: Experience Cloud users are external, and they follow their own rules. **Customer Community** users don't use roles, so you give them access with **sharing sets** (for example, all Cases on the user's Account) and **share groups**. **Partner** and **Customer Community Plus** users have roles and can be included in sharing rules. Guest users (people who aren't logged in) have the tightest rules: their OWD is always Private, and you share records to them only with guest user sharing rules. Watch for questions where an internal setting accidentally opens access to external users.

blocks.heading: Field and Object Security: Profiles vs Permission Sets
blocks.body: Record sharing decides which rows a user can see. Object and field permissions decide which objects and columns. Every user has one profile, and Salesforce recommends keeping it minimal and adding access with **permission sets** and **permission set groups**. A muting permission set inside a group can remove a permission the group would otherwise grant. Field-level security hides a field everywhere, including reports, list views and the API. Restriction rules go the other way from sharing: they filter which records a user can see even if sharing would allow more.

blocks.heading: Sharing Performance and Audit
blocks.body: Sharing gets slow when one user owns a huge number of records (ownership skew) or one parent record has thousands of child records (account data skew). Both cause long sharing recalculations and record locking. Fixes include spreading ownership across several users, placing integration users high or outside the role hierarchy, and using **Defer Sharing Calculations** during large data changes. For audits, use the Sharing button on a record to see why each user has access, Setup Audit Trail for configuration changes, and Field History Tracking or Shield Field Audit Trail for data changes.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Sharing and Visibility Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions come down to one thing: which setting gives exactly the access described, and no more. Read the scenario for who needs access, to which records, and whether they are internal or external.

blocks.heading: Access Evaluation Order
blocks.body: Work through it in order: object permission first, then OWD, then role hierarchy, sharing rules, teams and manual shares. If the object permission is missing, no sharing setting will help.

blocks.heading: Criteria-Based Sharing Rules
blocks.body: Use these when access depends on a field value, not on who owns the record. They can't use formula fields, and they re-run when the field changes.

blocks.heading: External Sharing Model
blocks.body: Customer Community users: sharing sets and share groups. Partner and Customer Community Plus users: roles and sharing rules. Guests: guest user sharing rules only.

blocks.heading: Performance Considerations
blocks.body: Watch for one owner with more than about 10,000 records, or one Account with more than about 10,000 child records. Both are signs of data skew.

blocks.heading: Apex Managed Sharing
blocks.body: Pick Apex sharing only when the rule is too complex for configuration, such as access based on a related record in another object. Use a custom sharing reason so the shares survive owner changes.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After Sharing and Visibility Architect, most people work toward Application Architect and then CTA:

sampleQuestions.question: Sales reps should only see Opportunities they own. Their managers should see their team's Opportunities. What is the right starting setup?
options: OWD Private with manual sharing on every record
OWD Public Read Only with a sharing rule for managers
OWD Private with the role hierarchy granting manager access
OWD Public Read/Write with field-level security
sampleQuestions.explanation: Private OWD hides other reps' records. The role hierarchy then lets each manager see what their team owns, with no extra rules.
whyWrong: Manual sharing on every record is slow, error-prone and is removed when the owner changes.
Public Read Only lets every rep see every Opportunity, which breaks the first requirement.
Field-level security hides fields, not records. Every rep could still open every Opportunity.

sampleQuestions.question: A user can see an Account in a list view but gets an error when opening a custom object record related to it. Sharing looks correct. What should the architect check first?
options: The Account sharing rules
The user's role
The org's Login IP ranges
The user's object permissions on the custom object
sampleQuestions.explanation: If a user has no Read permission on an object, no sharing setting can give them access. Object permission is always checked first.
whyWrong: Account sharing is already working, since the user can see the Account.
The role affects record access, but the error here points to the object itself.
Login IP ranges would block the whole login, not one object.

sampleQuestions.question: All Cases with Region set to EMEA must be visible to the EMEA Support public group, no matter who owns them. What should be used?
options: Changing Case OWD to Public Read Only
A Case team on every record
A criteria-based sharing rule on Case
An owner-based sharing rule on Case
sampleQuestions.explanation: The access depends on a field value, not on the owner. That is exactly what a criteria-based sharing rule does.
whyWrong: Public Read Only would open every Case to everyone, not just EMEA Support.
Adding a team to every Case by hand doesn't scale and is easy to miss.
Owner-based rules share by who owns the record, and the owners here vary.

sampleQuestions.question: Customer Community users should see all Cases related to their own Account. Customer Community users don't have roles. What should the architect use?
options: A sharing set based on the user's Account
A permission set with View All on Case
A criteria-based sharing rule for the community users
The role hierarchy
sampleQuestions.explanation: Sharing sets are built for this. They give Customer Community users access to records that match their Account or Contact.
whyWrong: View All would show every Case in the org, including other customers' Cases.
Customer Community users without roles can't be added to most sharing rules.
These users have no roles, so the role hierarchy doesn't apply.

sampleQuestions.question: An integration user owns 2 million Account records. Updates to the role hierarchy now take hours to process. What is the most likely cause?
options: Too many profiles in the org
Ownership data skew on the integration user
Too many permission set groups
Field-level security on Account
sampleQuestions.explanation: When one user owns a huge number of records, every change to their role or groups forces Salesforce to recalculate sharing on all of those records.
whyWrong: The number of profiles doesn't affect sharing recalculation.
Permission set groups control object and field access, not record sharing.
Field-level security isn't part of record sharing calculations.

sampleQuestions.question: Project records must be shared with every user listed in a related Project Member object. The list changes often. What should the architect recommend?
options: An owner-based sharing rule
Setting Project OWD to Public Read/Write
Apex managed sharing with a custom sharing reason
Manual sharing by the project owner
sampleQuestions.explanation: The access depends on records in another object, which sharing rules can't express. Apex managed sharing can, and a custom reason keeps the shares when the owner changes.
whyWrong: Owner-based rules can't read a list of members from another object.
Public Read/Write gives everyone access, not just project members.
Manual sharing depends on someone remembering to do it, and it is removed on owner change.

sampleQuestions.question: A manager in the role hierarchy should NOT automatically see records of a custom object owned by their team. What setting should be changed?
options: Remove Read permission on the object from the manager's profile
Remove the manager's role
Add a restriction rule for the manager
Uncheck Grant Access Using Hierarchies on that custom object
sampleQuestions.explanation: Grant Access Using Hierarchies can be turned off for custom objects. Managers then get no automatic access through the role hierarchy for that object.
whyWrong: Removing Read permission stops the manager seeing any of these records, including their own.
Removing the role affects every object, not just this one.
Restriction rules could work, but turning off hierarchy access is simpler and is the intended setting.

sampleQuestions.question: Which statement about org-wide defaults is correct?
options: Sharing rules can make access more restrictive than OWD
External OWD can't be more open than internal OWD
Permission sets can override OWD for single records
Internal OWD can be more restrictive than external OWD
sampleQuestions.explanation: External users can never get a broader default than internal users. You can set external defaults to be the same or more private.
whyWrong: Sharing rules only add access. They never take it away.
Permission sets grant object and field access. Only View All or Modify All bypass sharing, and they apply to the whole object.
It is the other way round: external defaults must be equal to or stricter than internal ones.

sampleQuestions.question: Partner users need to see Opportunities owned by other users at their own partner company, but not at other partner companies. What is the best approach?
options: Set Opportunity OWD to Public Read Only
Share using the partner account's roles in a sharing rule
Use a sharing set
Give partner users the View All Opportunities permission
sampleQuestions.explanation: Partner users get roles under their partner account. A sharing rule can share records owned by a partner account's roles with the other users in that same account.
whyWrong: Public Read Only would show all Opportunities to all partners.
Sharing sets are for Customer Community users, not partner users.
View All would show every Opportunity in the org.

sampleQuestions.question: Because of an old sharing rule, reps can see every record of a custom Invoice object. The business now wants reps to see only Invoices for their own country, without redesigning the sharing model. What feature fits?
options: A muting permission set
A restriction rule
A criteria-based sharing rule
Field-level security
sampleQuestions.explanation: Restriction rules filter the records a user can see, even when sharing would allow more. They are the only tool here that removes record visibility.
whyWrong: Muting permission sets remove object or field permissions, not record visibility.
Sharing rules only add access, so they can't narrow what a rep already sees.
Field-level security hides fields, not records.

sampleQuestions.question: Anonymous visitors to a public Experience Cloud site need to read published Knowledge-style records from a custom object. How is access given?
options: Create a guest user sharing rule
Add the guest user to the role hierarchy
Set the object's external OWD to Public Read Only
Add the guest user to a public group
sampleQuestions.explanation: Guest users always have Private OWD. The only way to share records with them is a guest user sharing rule.
whyWrong: Guest users don't have roles.
Guest users are locked to Private and can't use more open defaults.
Guest users can't be added to regular public groups for sharing.

sampleQuestions.question: A rep shares an Opportunity manually with a colleague. Later the Opportunity is reassigned to a new owner. What happens to the manual share?
options: It is kept and moved to the new owner
It is kept only if the colleague is in the same role
It becomes a sharing rule
It is removed
sampleQuestions.explanation: Manual shares are deleted when the record owner changes. Apex managed sharing with a custom reason is the way to keep shares through owner changes.
whyWrong: Manual shares are not carried over to a new owner.
The colleague's role doesn't matter. The share is removed either way.
Manual shares never turn into sharing rules.

sampleQuestions.question: A company is about to load 5 million records and change several sharing rules. They want to avoid long sharing recalculations during the load. What should they use?
options: Turn off the role hierarchy
Change all OWD to Public Read/Write
Defer Sharing Calculations
Delete all sharing rules and recreate them
sampleQuestions.explanation: Defer Sharing Calculations pauses recalculation while you make changes, then runs it once at the end.
whyWrong: You can't turn off the role hierarchy for standard objects, and it would change access for everyone.
Opening OWD would expose data to everyone, even for a short time.
Deleting and recreating rules causes two big recalculations instead of one.

sampleQuestions.question: A support agent should be able to edit the Status field on Cases but never see the Customer SSN field on Contact. Which tool controls the SSN requirement?
options: Field-level security
Org-wide defaults
A sharing rule
The role hierarchy
sampleQuestions.explanation: Field-level security controls whether a user can see or edit a field. It hides the field in pages, reports, list views and the API.
whyWrong: OWD sets record access, not field visibility.
Sharing rules control records, not fields.
The role hierarchy controls record access, not fields.

sampleQuestions.question: Auditors ask why a specific user can see a specific Account. What is the fastest way to find out?
options: Use the Sharing Hierarchy button on the Account record
Run a report on the user's profile
Export all sharing rules and read them
Check the user's login history
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Sharing Hierarchy button on a record lists the users who can access it and the reason for each, such as a role, a sharing rule or a team.
whyWrong: A profile report shows object permissions, not why one record is visible.
Reading every rule by hand is slow and can miss teams or manual shares.
Login history shows when someone logged in, not why they have access.
